title: The offering

lines: BREAD AND WINE UP THE AISLE.
cards: A wicker basket on the end of a long wooden pole swings down the row, and a little girl drops in a coin she's held so tightly it's warm. Across town, a plate goes hand to hand, and someone slips in an envelope.
In a third church, a family carries a plate of bread and a small jug of wine up the center aisle and hands them to the priest. In a fourth, just a box by the door.
Different churches, one moment: something is carried forward. Today: the offering.

teach.b: Two kinds of gift come forward at the offering: money for the church and the poor, and, where communion is celebrated that day, bread and wine for the table, sometimes carried up from the pews.
In the Orthodox liturgy they're carried through the church in a slow procession called the Great Entrance. The idea underneath both comes from King David.
In First Chronicles, the people have just given freely toward building the temple, gold and silver and more. David doesn't congratulate them.

teach.h: OF THINE OWN HAVE WE GIVEN THEE.
teach.b: He blesses God: "But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly after this sort? for all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee." It turns giving inside out.
Nothing was theirs to begin with; they hand back what they were handed.
Some churches say that line as the gifts come forward, and the Orthodox liturgy, as the bread and wine are lifted up, says something close: thine own of thine own. Then the size of a gift.
In Mark, Jesus sits near the temple treasury, watching. Rich people put in much.

teach.h: THE WIDOW GAVE MORE THAN ALL.
teach.b: A poor widow puts in two small coins, and Jesus says, "this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury." They gave from what they had left over. She gave all she had.
And the spirit of it: Paul writes, "God loveth a cheerful giver." Not grudgingly, he says, and not because you have to.

how: In many churches an offering of money is collected during the service, by plate, basket or box, and where communion is celebrated the bread and wine are brought to the table at this point; in the Orthodox Divine Liturgy they are carried in procession in the Great Entrance.

games.q: you're sitting with Jesus near the temple treasury, watching people give. he calls you over. who does he say gave the most?
o: the rich people who put in large sums.
the poor widow who put in two small coins.
nobody: he says giving doesn't matter.
games.why: the widow. the others gave from what they had left over; she gave all she had.

practice: Turn your hands palm up on your knees, and let a few things you were given come to mind: this breath, a person who taught you, a meal.

Then choose one small gift to pass on, some money, an hour, a meal for a neighbor, and decide it now. If you pray, you can say David's words: all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee.

wordCard.voice: The offering. The moment when gifts and bread are carried forward, handing back to God what Christians say was God's to begin with.

orig.note: Greek, from the Orthodox Divine Liturgy: thine own of thine own, said as the bread and wine are offered.

carryVoice: Your line: all things come of thee. Two small coins can be more than all. Until tomorrow.
